title: Mills, Factories and Smoky Cities
summary: Long ago, people spun thread and wove cloth at home. Then giant mills full of machines appeared, first beside rivers and then, thanks to steam engines, right in the middle of cities like Manchester. One huge engine could turn hundreds of machines, and life began to run by the factory clock.

sections.heading: Spinning by the Fireside
paragraphs: Step into a farmhouse in Lancashire in about 1750. In the corner, a woman sits at a spinning wheel, drawing out fluffy fibres of cotton or wool and twisting them into thread. Her children card the raw fibre, combing it into soft rolls ready for spinning. In the next room, her husband works a wooden handloom, throwing the shuttle back and forth to weave cloth. Nobody tells them when to start or stop. They work around the farm chores, the seasons and the daylight.

This was the cottage industry, also called the domestic or putting-out system. A merchant, sometimes called a clothier, delivered raw fibre to families in villages, came back later to collect the yarn or finished cloth, and paid them for each piece. Spinning was slow. It took several spinners to keep a single weaver busy, and as weavers got faster with John Kay's flying shuttle, invented in 1733, the shortage of yarn grew worse.

Then came a burst of inventions. James Hargreaves's spinning jenny, from the mid-1760s, let one person spin several threads at once, but it was still small and hand-powered, so it fitted in a cottage. Richard Arkwright's water frame, patented in 1769, was different. It spun strong cotton thread using sets of rollers, and it needed more power than a person could supply. Samuel Crompton's 'mule' of 1779 combined ideas from both and spun very fine, strong yarn. These machines were too big, too many and too power-hungry for a cottage. They needed a new kind of building, filled with machines and workers, driven by one central source of power. They needed a factory.

sections.heading: Arkwright's Mill by the River
paragraphs: Richard Arkwright was born in Preston in 1732, the youngest of a large and poor family, and began his working life as a barber and wig-maker. He was not a great inventor in the way Watt was. Historians argue about how much of the water frame he designed himself, and some of his patents were later overturned in court. But he was a brilliant organiser and businessman, and he understood that machines, buildings, workers and money could be combined into a system.

In 1771 Arkwright and his partners built a cotton-spinning mill at Cromford in Derbyshire, in a steep valley of the River Derwent. He chose the spot carefully. A stream of water flowed out of the Cromford Sough, a tunnel that drained the nearby lead mines, and it joined the Bonsall Brook. Because the water came from deep underground, it is said to have rarely frozen in winter, so the waterwheel could turn all year. The wheel turned shafts and gears that drove rows of water frames on several floors.

The first mill was five storeys high. It started with about 200 workers, most of them women and children. The youngest children were reportedly as young as seven, though Arkwright later raised the minimum age to ten. From 1772 the mill ran day and night in two shifts of twelve hours each. The gates were shut at six in the morning and six in the evening, and workers who arrived late were locked out, losing a day's pay and fined another day's pay on top.

Cromford was in the countryside, and there were not enough local people to run it, so Arkwright built houses for workers, which still stand on North Street, as well as a chapel, a market and later a school. Families moved there from far away, and he especially liked families with many children who could work in the mill. By the time Arkwright died in 1792, he employed about 1,000 workers at Cromford and had become one of the richest men in Britain. The Derwent Valley Mills are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Notice something about Cromford, though. It was in a narrow valley, miles from big towns, because that is where the falling water was. Water-powered factories had to be built beside fast rivers and streams, often in remote places. Raw cotton had to be hauled in and finished yarn hauled out along bad roads. And in a dry summer, or a hard frost, the wheels might slow or stop. If only a factory could make its own power anywhere it liked.

sections.heading: The Engine Moves into the Mill
paragraphs: The first steps were cautious. In the early 1780s Arkwright himself opened a cotton mill, Shudehill Mill on Miller Street in Manchester, close to the markets and the workers. It used a steam engine, but in an indirect way: the engine pumped water up to a reservoir so it could flow back down and turn an ordinary waterwheel. It was inefficient, but it shows how badly mill owners wanted to escape the riverbank.

After 1782, Boulton and Watt's new rotative engines, which could turn a shaft directly using the sun-and-planet gear described in Part 9, made a far better solution possible. In 1785 the Robinson family, who ran cotton mills at Papplewick in Nottinghamshire, installed a Boulton and Watt rotative engine to drive their spinning machinery. It is generally recognised as the first steam engine to power a cotton mill directly. According to local accounts, the Robinsons had a special reason: a local landowner had been changing the flow of water upstream for his ornamental lakes, leaving their waterwheels short of water. Steam gave them independence.

Other mill owners soon followed, including Arkwright and his partners and the new spinning firms of Manchester. By 1800 Boulton and Watt had supplied dozens of engines to cotton and other textile mills, and many cheaper engines built by rival makers were at work too. After the Watt patent expired in 1800, local engineering firms in Lancashire began building mill engines in great numbers.

The change this made was enormous, but simple to state. With a steam engine, a factory could be built wherever there was coal, workers, roads, canals and customers. It no longer needed a waterfall. Mills began to cluster in towns, especially on the coalfields of Lancashire and Yorkshire, and in places served by canals, which could bring coal cheaply. The Bridgewater Canal, opened in 1761 to carry coal from the Duke of Bridgewater's mines at Worsley into Manchester, had already halved the price of coal there. Cheap coal plus steam engines plus thousands of workers turned Manchester into the most famous factory town on Earth.

sections.heading: One Engine, a Thousand Machines
paragraphs: How could one steam engine run hundreds of spinning machines spread across five or six floors? The answer was a system of spinning rods and belts called line shafting, sometimes called millwork.

The engine usually lived in its own tall engine house at the side or end of the mill, next to the boiler house and its chimney. Its great flywheel, sometimes many metres across, turned a main shaft. In many mills, the power went up through the building by a vertical shaft with gears at each floor. Later mills often used a 'rope race', a narrow tower where thick cotton ropes ran in grooves from the flywheel up to each floor, like a giant drive belt.

On each floor, a long iron shaft ran along the ceiling, hanging from brackets, turning steadily the whole length of the room. Fixed to it were pulleys, wheels with a flat or curved rim. A loop of leather belt ran down from each pulley to a pulley on a machine below. Big pulleys and small pulleys could change the speed, just as gears on a bicycle do. To stop one machine without stopping the whole mill, a worker shifted its belt sideways onto a 'loose pulley' that spun freely without driving anything.

Line shafting was clever, but it had problems. Every bearing, gear and belt wasted some power through friction, and in many systems a quarter or more of the engine's power was lost before it reached the machines. The belts flapped and slapped, the shafts rumbled, oil dripped from the bearings, and the air was thick with cotton fluff. Worst of all, the moving belts and shafts were unguarded for a long time, and workers, including children, could have hair, sleeves or hands caught, causing terrible injuries.

Imagine standing on the floor of a big spinning room in about 1840. The room is as long as a football pitch, lit by rows of tall windows. Above your head, the shaft turns with a low hum. Dozens of belts slant down to the mules, which roll forward and back across the floor, drawing out and twisting hundreds of threads at a time. The air is warm and damp, because cotton thread breaks less easily in moist air, and fluff drifts like snow. The noise is so loud that many workers learned to talk by lip-reading, a habit some kept for the rest of their lives.

Because the whole mill hung on one engine, the engine was precious. Mill engines were often beautifully painted and polished, with brass fittings and decorative columns, and owners sometimes gave them names, often after members of their family. The engine tenter, the worker who looked after it, was an important person. If the engine stopped, the whole mill fell silent and nobody earned anything. Line shafts stayed in use until the early 1900s, when factories gradually switched to electric motors, often one on each machine, powered by electricity that, as later parts explain, was itself usually made with steam.

sections.heading: Cottonopolis
paragraphs: In the 1770s, Manchester was a busy market town with a few tens of thousands of people. By 1851 it had over 300,000, and the surrounding towns had grown just as fast. People poured in from the countryside of Lancashire and Cheshire, from Ireland, from Scotland and beyond, looking for work. In the 1800s Manchester gained a new nickname: Cottonopolis, the city of cotton.

Raw cotton arrived by ship at Liverpool, much of it grown on plantations in the southern United States by enslaved people, a dark connection explored in Part 15. It came up to Manchester by canal, and later by rail, to be spun and woven. Manchester's own cotton mills peaked at more than 100 in the 1850s, and as land in the city grew expensive, many more were built in nearby towns such as Oldham, Bolton, Rochdale, Stockport and Blackburn. Manchester itself became the great trading centre, packed with warehouses, banks and the Royal Exchange where cotton was bought and sold. By 1871, Manchester and its surrounding towns produced about a third of all the cotton goods in the world.

The district of Ancoats, beside the Rochdale Canal, became one of the world's first industrial suburbs. Huge mills such as Murrays' Mills, built from the late 1790s, rose six or seven storeys high, with tall chimneys pouring out coal smoke. A visitor arriving by night saw rows of mill windows blazing with light, and in the day saw a sky stained brown and grey.

Visitors came from all over the world to see this new kind of city. The French writer Alexis de Tocqueville, who visited in 1835, described Manchester as a place where human industry produced astonishing wealth and, side by side with it, shocking poverty, with filthy water running through the streets and the sun seen dimly through the smoke. Many visitors felt both excitement and alarm: this was the future, but was it a good one?

The smoke itself was a sign of steam. Every mill had its own boiler house burning coal day after day, and a mill chimney might stand 60 metres or more tall to carry the fumes away and to create a strong draught for the fire. Hundreds of chimneys together blackened buildings, washing hung out to dry and people's lungs. Rivers such as the Irwell and the Medlock carried dyes, sewage and waste from works along their banks. Cleaner air laws came only much later.

The workers had to live somewhere close, because they walked to work. Builders threw up rows of cheap houses as fast as they could, often 'back-to-backs', where two houses shared a back wall and had windows on only one side. Some of the poorest families lived in damp cellars. Streets were unpaved, drains were few, and many houses shared a single toilet or privy. Diseases such as cholera and typhus spread easily, and in the worst districts many children did not live past the age of five. In 1845 a young German, Friedrich Engels, published a famous description of these conditions. Part 15 looks at that dark side in more detail.

Yet the same cities were also full of energy and new ideas. Manchester produced engineers, scientists, newspapers, libraries, mechanics' institutes where workers could study in the evenings, and political movements that campaigned for votes and fairer laws. The scientist John Dalton, who developed atomic theory, taught in Manchester, and James Joule, whose work you will meet in Part 16, grew up nearby in Salford, the son of a brewer.

sections.heading: Living by the Clock
paragraphs: Perhaps the deepest change factories brought was a change in time itself. A handloom weaver at home could work hard for a few days and rest for one, start late, or stop to help with the harvest. In a steam mill, the engine started at a fixed hour and every machine began turning together. Workers had to be at their machines when it did.

So factory life ran by the clock and the bell. Mill bells or, later, steam whistles called workers in the early morning. Some towns had 'knocker-uppers', people paid to tap on bedroom windows with long poles to wake workers before dawn, since few families owned clocks. Gates were locked at the starting time, and latecomers were fined or sent home without pay. Inside, overseers enforced rules with fines for talking, whistling, opening a window or leaving a machine.

Days were long. In the early 1800s, twelve to fourteen hours a day, six days a week, was common, with short breaks for meals. Children were valued because they were cheap and small. 'Piecers' walked up and down beside spinning mules, joining broken threads, while 'scavengers' crawled underneath the moving machines to sweep away fluff. Many children were 'pauper apprentices', orphans or children of very poor families sent from parish workhouses to mills, where they lived in apprentice houses. Laws limiting children's work came slowly, starting in the early 1800s, as Part 15 describes.

Mill owners argued that discipline was necessary. A steam engine burned coal whether the machines were working or not, and expensive machinery earned money only while it was running, so every idle minute cost the owner. That is why owners wanted engines running as many hours as possible and why fines for lateness were so harsh. Some owners, such as Robert Owen at New Lanark in Scotland in the early 1800s, tried a different approach, refusing to employ very young children, providing schools and better housing, and showing that a mill could still make a profit. Owen's ideas inspired reformers, though few owners copied him fully.

Workers did not simply accept all this. They formed friendly societies to help each other when sick, campaigned for a ten-hour day, and organised early trade unions. Over the 1800s, hours slowly fell, the Saturday half-holiday spread, and by the late 1800s many mill towns shut down for a whole 'wakes week' each summer, when families crowded onto trains to seaside resorts such as Blackpool. The rhythm of modern life, with fixed working hours, weekends and holidays, grew partly out of the factory clock.

sections.heading: Water Doesn't Give Up
paragraphs: It would be easy to imagine that once steam appeared, every waterwheel stopped. That is not what happened. Water power was free once a wheel was built, while coal cost money every day. For decades, many mill owners stuck with water, and some used both, with a steam engine to help out when the river ran low.

Waterwheels kept getting better, too. Engineers built big iron wheels, some more than 20 metres across, and in 1827 the French engineer Benoit Fourneyron built an efficient water turbine, a forerunner of the turbines in today's hydroelectric dams. In the United States, the great textile city of Lowell in Massachusetts, founded in the 1820s, was built around canals and water power from the Merrimack River. Historians estimate that in Britain water still provided a large share of factory power into the 1830s, and steam did not clearly overtake it until around the middle of the 1800s. In America, water power stayed important even longer.

Many mill owners treated the two kinds of power as partners rather than rivals. A mill might run its waterwheel whenever the river was full and start up a small steam engine in dry summers or icy winters, so the machines never had to stop. Some engines were even used to pump water back up above the wheel, the trick Arkwright had tried in Manchester. In hilly districts of Yorkshire and Scotland, where fast streams were plentiful and coal was far away, water-powered mills kept working well into the late 1800s.

What tipped the balance was a combination of things: steam engines that used less coal, cheaper coal carried by canals and railways, mills in towns with no good rivers, and factories growing so large that no stream could drive them. The Industrial Revolution was a gradual change, not a sudden switch, and steam took over step by step through the 1800s.

sections.heading: The Giant of Philadelphia
paragraphs: Steam's spread to America brought fresh ideas. George Henry Corliss was born in New York State in 1817 and set up an engine works in Providence, Rhode Island. On 10 March 1849 he received a US patent for a new kind of valve gear. Instead of one sliding valve doing every job, a Corliss engine had four separate valves, one to let steam in and one to let it out at each end of the cylinder. They snapped open and shut quickly, and, cleverly, the engine's governor decided exactly when to cut off the steam on each stroke. If the load was light, steam was cut off early; if a mill suddenly needed more power, it was cut off later. Some historians note that a similar idea had been developed earlier by another American engineer, Frederick Sickels.

Corliss engines kept a very steady speed, which mattered in mills where an uneven speed could snap threads, and they used roughly 30 percent less fuel than ordinary engines of the time. Corliss even offered to be paid from the coal savings, a sales trick that echoes Boulton and Watt. His engines were copied all over the world and drove mills, waterworks and, later, electric generators.

His most famous engine was built for a party. In 1876 the United States celebrated 100 years since the Declaration of Independence with the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia. At its heart was Machinery Hall, filled with lathes, looms, printing presses, pumps and saws. Rather than give each one its own engine, the organisers had a single giant Corliss engine drive the whole hall through about a mile of overhead line shafting.

The Centennial Engine was a twin-cylinder beam engine that stood about 45 feet (14 metres) tall, with a flywheel 30 feet (about 9 metres) across. It produced about 1,400 horsepower. On 10 May 1876, President Ulysses S. Grant and Emperor Pedro II of Brazil turned the controls, and the great beams began to rock and the flywheel to turn, setting hundreds of machines in motion. Visitors were amazed at how quietly and smoothly it ran. Many people said it was the star of the whole exhibition.

After the fair, the engine went back to Providence, and about seven years later it was sold to the railway-carriage builder George Pullman to drive his factory near Chicago, where it worked until 1910 before being scrapped. By then, the world had changed. A hundred years earlier, a factory had been a mill by a stream in Derbyshire. Now steam drove whole halls of machines in a country that had barely existed when Watt patented his condenser.

And steam was not changing only cotton mills. It was blowing air into blast furnaces to make iron, driving hammers and lathes that made more machines, printing newspapers by the thousand, and reshaping whole countries. Historians have a name for that great transformation, and it is where we go next: the Industrial Revolution.

deepDive: Historians argue about how important steam really was to the early factory system. The first great factories, like Arkwright's Cromford Mill (1771) and Jedediah Strutt's mills at Belper, ran on water, and the factory as a way of organising work, with central power, supervision, shifts and discipline, existed before steam took over. Economic historians who have counted horsepower find that water remained a major source of industrial power in Britain into the 1830s, and steam's share grew decisively only in the middle decades of the century, helped by more efficient high-pressure and compound engines, cheaper coal carried by canals and railways, and ever-larger mills. Some, such as the economic historian Nicholas Crafts, have estimated that steam's measurable contribution to British economic growth was modest before about 1830 and much larger afterwards. So steam did not create the factory, but it set the factory free from geography, letting mills concentrate on coalfields and in cities like Manchester, Oldham and Bolton. That concentration had huge social effects: rapid urban growth, crowded and unhealthy housing, and new patterns of work and time. The historian E. P. Thompson's famous essay on 'time, work-discipline and industrial capitalism' (1967) argued that the factory clock reshaped people's sense of time itself. Engineering-wise, line-shaft drive was a hidden cost: friction in shafts, gears and belts often consumed a quarter or more of an engine's output, which is one reason electric motors, which could be placed on each machine, spread rapidly after about 1900. In America, the Corliss valve gear (patented 1849) was a key step, combining automatic variable cut-off with quick-acting valves to give steady speed and fuel savings of roughly 30 percent over fixed cut-off engines. The 1,400-horsepower Centennial Engine of 1876 became a symbol of American industrial confidence, even as most of its power was spent turning shafting rather than machines.
funFact: At the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, a single Corliss steam engine about 14 metres tall powered the machines of the entire Machinery Hall through roughly a mile of overhead shafting.
